appendix.title: Create SSL/TLS keys and certificates with openssl
appendix.para: In the following we will create our own CA (Certification agency) that will sign all our public keys. This means that to avoid the warnings in browsers about untrusted certificate the CA certificate (our root certificate) should be imported into the browsers. As an example we will show how this is done for the Chrome browser at the end of this appendix.

The main purpose of this section is to show how the bare bones “openssl” command can be used to create certificates rather than relying on the simple but somewhat magical utility scripts we used in the main discussion. We recommend that one you have gotten over the initial chock of dealing with certificates this is actually a simpler method.

As convention we will use the extension *.pem for all keys (since this is the format they keys are in). To distinguish between the public (the certificate) and private key we will add “_public” and “_private” to the main name of the key-pair.

Some documentation uses the suffix “*.crt” and “*.key” for the public and private key in PEM format. However, our opinion is that the suffix should reflect the format of the file (in this case the PEM) format and the use of crt and key as suffixes make things unnecessary complicated. Especially since one might believe that “*.crt” and “*.key” are in themselves are new formats.
At the end of this walk-though we will have to generate the following key-pairs to use in our setup

listitem.para: This is our own “Root” certificate. This public key is implicitly trusted, i.e. it is trusted because we say so. No higher authority (but us) has sanctioned this key pair.
This is the keypair we will use with Apache when https connections are made
This is the keypair that will be used for both Dovecot2 as well as postfix to encrypt both IMAP and SMTP protocols into IMAPS and SMTPS
This is a keypair which makes it possible to access the server under several aliases. This if further described in section E.5

appendix.para: In the process of generating these targets there will also be some intermediate files that strictly speaking is not necessary to keep (but might come in handy later on as we shall see).
The process is now as follows

listitem.para: Create the CA key-pair as a root certificate, i.e. it will be “signed” by itself. It is trusted because we say so!
Handle the key-pair for https
Create the key-pair, private and public key
Prepare the public key to be signed by creating the “Certificate signing request” (CSR) based on the public key
Sign the public key with our CA private key
Handle the key-pair for dovecot and postfix
Create the key-pair, private and public key
Prepare the public key to be signed by creating the “Certificate signing request” (CSR) based on the public key
c. Sign the public key with our CA private key

appendix.para: Please read through the above steps again and make sure you understand the principle. (In practice the creation of the key-pair and the signing request is done in one step – but logically they are separate.)

caution.para: There is no shortage of description on the net on how to create so called self-signed certificates. However many of them are dated and based on very old ways of doing things which have just been inherited out of laziness and without propre understanding of the tools involved.

For example, many descriptions do not add the “-nodes” flag as we do in these examples. This will force a password to be created for the private key in certificates and since this is usually not wanted (as described below) one extra step is then required to remove the password. Hence making the description unnecessarily complicated. Another example of obsoleted usage is the option “nsCertType = server” in config files. This option is since long superseded and is not even necessary in our context. Again, adding complexity where none is needed. Another (very popular) complexity adder is to create the private key separately from the certificate request with another obsoleted command; “openssl genrsa”.

Yet another plain wrong way that many HowTo:s show is to create the initial serial number for the certificates in the database (that “openssl ca” keeps of all signed certificates ) by simply storing a number one in a file (usually by “echo 01 > serial”). Instead the option “-create_serial” should be given to let openssl initialize a random 128 bit serial number.

Dealing with SSL/TLS certificate introduces many new terms and takes a while getting used to especially since “openssl” is not exactly easy to use. It has evolved (together with the standards) for a long time and old options that are since long superseded remains. However, there is no need to make things more black magic than necessary and the way we show below is what we believe the absolute easiest way to accomplish what we need in the minimum number of steps.

sect1.title: The use of the term “self-signed certificates”
sect1.para: The term self-signed certificate has two distinct meanings. It could mean that we sign a certificate that we have generated our self with our own CA (root) certificate that we have either created (most likely) or bought (highly unlikely). This is the way we use the term self-signed certificate in this appendix.

It could also mean that we create a CA-type certificate which is (almost) a regular certificate that it not signed by anyone but have a flag inside it that says “trust me, because I say so – I’m a root certificate”. This is really what openssl means by self-signing, the certificate is signed by itself.
Many of the tools out there create this latter type of certificate to avoid having to create a separate CA (root certificate)

sect1.title: Preparations
sect1.para: When reading the description below you need to watch out for the order of the argument to openssl. Sometimes it doesn’t matter but sometimes it does and the error message you get will not really be helpful. For example, calling “openssl req -new –nodes . . .“ will work but calling “openssl req –nodes –new . . . ” will not work and fail with an error message about unrecognized option “-nodes”. While logically this could be explained it’s not really helpful if you are not used to the idiosyncrasies of openssl. While we could use the default “/etc/ssl” as our working directory we do not recommend this. Instead we create a pristine directory with our own setup so we won’t disturb anything else. Later on it is also easy to create a safety backup of this directory. We will therefore create a new directory which we will use to hold all keys and intermediate files. Since openssl keeps track of all certificates we have signed by means of a simple textual database (and a serial number) we must also setup those initial helper files.
In this directory we will have four additional subdirectories:

listitem.para: “private” , Stores all private keys we create
“public”, Stores all public keys (signed certificates)
“csr” , Stores all certificate signing requests (public keys which have not yet been signed)
“newcerts”, Stores a copy all our signed certificates (the “openssl ca” command will automatically store a copy of all signed certificate in this directory).

sect1.para: Start by creating this directory structure as (we will name our root directory “ca”):
sect1.screen: $> mkdir ca $> cd ca $> mkdir private $> mkdir public $> mkdir csr $> mkdir newcerts
sect1.para: Now we create an empty file which later on will hod the the simple text database which “openssl ca” uses to keep track of all certificates that we sign (openssl will complain if this file doesn’t exist).

We shall now create a config file for openssl. One way to do this would be to take the supplied standard openssl config file (in /etc/ssl) and modify a few lines. However, we will create our own smaller version so that we now the exact meaning of every single line we have in the config file. This config file will also have some useful defaults to save us some typing each time we create (or sign) a certificate. We will therefore create our own minimal “our_openssl.cnf” as follows (you should probably name this file after your site and remember to use that name in the commands that follows for clarity).
sect1.programlisting:
#====================================================================== # Simplified openssl config file based on distributed openssl file # Version 1.0 #======================================================================
####################################################################### # CA Definitions – point to section where all default values can be # found. [ ca ] default_ca = CA_default
####################################################################### # "openssl ca" default parameters [ CA_default ]
dir = . new_certs_dir = $dir/newcerts database = $dir/index.txt certificate = $dir/public/ca_public.pem # Our CA (root) certificate (public key) private_key = $dir/private/ca_private.pem # The private key for our CA key-pair serial = $dir/serial
# In our case we will not really be using Certificate Revocation Lists # but we include the setup for future use crldir = $dir/crl crlnumber = $dir/crlnumber crl = $crldir/crl.pem
default_days = 3650 # We sign certificates that are valid for ~10 years default_md = sha1 # The sha1 encryption method is recommended over the older md5 name_opt = ca_default cert_opt = ca_default preserve = no policy = policy_match
x509_extensions = usr_cert copy_extensions = copy # Honor the certificatre
#################################################################### # The default policy for the CA when signing requests We only request # that certificate is from the same country [ policy_match ] countryName = match stateOrProvinceName = supplied organizationName = supplied organizationalUnitName = supplied commonName = supplied emailAddress = supplied
####################################################################### #Default values for use with “openssl req” command [ req ] default_bits = 2048 default_md = sha1 string_mask = utf8only distinguished_name = req_distinguished_name req_extensions = v3_req # Extensions to add when creating certificate requests x509_extensions = v3_ca # Extensions to add to self-signed certificates
####################################################################### # Prompts and default values for the fields in the DN [ req_distinguished_name ] 0.organizationName = Organization Name 0.organizationName_default = Aditus
organizationalUnitName = Unit or department in organization organizationalUnitName_default = IT-Adm
emailAddress = Email Address emailAddress_max = 64 emailAddress_default = admin@aditus.nu
localityName = City or district localityName_default = Sundbyberg
stateOrProvinceName = State or Province Name stateOrProvinceName_default = Sundbyberg
countryName = Country Code (2 letter code) countryName_min = 2 countryName_max = 2 countryName_default = SE
commonName = Common Name (hostname, IP, or your name) commonName_max = 64
####################################################################### # Extension values used when signing certificates as a CA [ usr_cert ] basicConstraints=CA:false subjectKeyIdentifier=hash authorityKeyIdentifier=keyid,issuer
####################################################################### # For the normal case where we do not create CA certificate but only # ordinary client certificates [ v3_req ] basicConstraints=CA:false subjectKeyIdentifier=hash
# Uncomment the following if you want the certificate request generated on this server # to have several aliases for the common name. Unfortunately this parameter can not be # given on the command line. # (Alternatively this could be specified as “subjectAltName = DNS:example.com, # DNS:www.example.com” instead as a list as we have done it now. # subjectAltName = @alt_names
# Alias name for this server when creating signing requests. These are just examples!! # Uncomment the following section and set proper names #[ alt_names ] #DNS.1 = sigma1 #DNS.2 = sigma1.nil
####################################################################### # Section to be added when we give the command line option -extensions v3_ca # together with the x509 option meaning that this should be a self-signed # certificate, i.e CA=TRUE [ v3_ca ] basicConstraints = CA:TRUE subjectKeyIdentifier = hash authorityKeyIdentifier = keyid:always,issuer:always
#EOF

sect1.title: Generating the CA key-pair
sect1.para: We are now in position to generate our root (CA) certificate. The first step is to create the key-pair and the signing request
The next step is for us to sign it our self
sect1.screen: $> openssl ca -create_serial -out public/ca_public.pem -selfsign -extensions v3_ca \ -config our_openssl.cnf -days 7000 -infiles csr/ca_public_req.pem
sect1.para: This will prompt you for a number of things most of them have default values as specified in the config file. Do not forget the password you gave here for the CA private key.
The special options used for the CA signing as compared to all the signings we will do from here on are he two options

listitem.para: -selfsign, Which tells openssl to use the ca_public_req.pem when signing instead of expecting a CA certificate (which we haven’t created yet)
-extension v3_ca, needed to read the v3_ca section in the config file.

sect1.para: Our CA certificate (root certificate) will be valid for roughly 20 years (~7000 days). We have now produced the following files:

listitem.para: private/ca_private.pem, The password protected private key part of our CA-key pair. This file should be kept secret at all times!
public/ca_public.pem, The public key that should be imported into browsers that we want to accept any other public leys (certificates) that we will sign in the future.
csr/ca_public_req.pem, The signing request for our CA
serial, This is an administrative file used by “openssl ca” to give a unique serial number for each of the certificate that we sign.

newcerts/<random_serial_number>.pem, A copy of our signed certificate. The exact name is random since it starts with the serial number that was randomly generated. From this moment on each serial number will be incremented by one for each new certificate that we sign.

sect1.para: Many other tutorials show what seems to be a simpler way to create root certificate in only one step using the –x509 option with openssl. As in
However, we do not recommend this way since it has a number of drawbacks:

listitem.para: You cannot use –create_serial with the “req” command
The signing request is not kept
There is no copy for our signed root certificate in newcerts as it is with all other cert we created

sect1.para: This could however be used in another way. If you need to quickly create a “test-certificate” (which isn’t signed by any trusted authority or yourself) you could create such a certificate in the same way (no need to include the –extensions v3_ca in this case though) such as
You can now use the resulting certificate if you need to run some quick test with some software that requires a SSL/TLS certificate (key-pair).

note.para: Note on x509v3 compliancy. The CA certificate we have created here is, while perfectly working, not formally fully compliant with the very latest version of the PKIX and X509v3 standards since that requires the email address to be specified in a slightly different place. This is however of no practical concern for us (unless you plan on starting your own worldwide certification agency and charge money for signing certificates)

sect1.title: Generating the Apache HTTPS key-pair
sect1.para: We will now generate the key-pair that will allow HTTPS traffic. We will show two ways of doing this. The first (and simplest) is top just generate a key-pair which is valid for exactly one common name, i.e. the name you access the browser with. On a home network where you probably don’t have a DNS server you will most likely access the server via an IP address directly. The problem with only having one name in the certificate is that if you access the browser through some other methods (perhaps from outside your router with a completely different IP address) you might again get a warning about untrusted site even if you have imported browser public key.

The following command will generate a key-pair. As you can see we have added the suffix “_req” to the public key. That is to remind ourself that this will just be used as a certificate signing request, i.e. this public key has not yet been signed by our CA key-pari created in the previous step. After we have signed the key it will be named “https_public.pem”

Answer all the questions that you are now presented with. Keep in mind that every certificate must have a unique distinguished name that is made up of the fields like company name, city, department/unit etc. A recommendation is therefore to use “Web” (or Apache or similar) as the unit name to differentiate this certificate from the other mail certificate we need to create as a next step.
For future reference you should save all requests and keys. The request can be re-used if the certificate has expired. So far we produced the following new files:

listitem.para: csr/https_public_req.pem, This is the public key that we will sign with our CA keys
private/https_private.pem, This is our private key that will be loaded by Apache

Answer the questions and use the password for the private CA key we created in section E.3. We have now generated the files

listitem.para: public/https_public.pem, This is the signed public certificate for Apache
newcerts/<some_large_serial_number>.pem, A copy for our own record of the just created certificate. The naming is the serial number of the certificate.

sect1.para: This newly signed certificate is also recorded in our database file “index”

sect1.title: Generating a certificate with multiple common names
sect1.para: As mentioned above most people create certificates as we did above. However, for the case the same server is accessed through many names (for example “www.myserver.com” or “myserver.com” or “199.243.243.12” etc) this certificate will still generate a warning if we access the server with any other name besides what we used when we created the certificate signing request. To create a certificate with multiple alternative names requires some additional setup. In the preparation section our “openssl.cnf” contains all the necessary parameters but we need to uncomment them. First uncomment the line
Then uncomment and setup the lines at the end of the file
sect1.screen:
subjectAltName = @alt_names
# Alias name for this server when creating signing requests. # These are just examples!! # Uncomment the following section and set proper names [alt_names] DNS.1 = example.com DNS.2 = www.example.com DNS.3 = 199.199.199.199
sect1.para: To match the values you want to have. The you can just generate the certificate as in the same way we did before (we just use a different name for the certificate to keep them apart)

We can view the request to make sure that we have the alternative names included with the command.

sect1.para: It is useful to know that if some servers only give you the option to specify one SSL/TLS file you must combine both the public (certificate) and the private key in one file. You can easily do this as

You could also do this for Dovecot and postfix since they will read the correct key based on the headers in the file. Some might think that this is better way of keeping out key-pair since we can never lose one key in the key-pair if we keep them combined.

sect1.title: Converting to other certificate formats
sect1.para: As mentioned previously there are other variant formats besides PEM used to store certificates and keys. More specifically there are two other formats commonly usedas described below.

sect2.title: DER format
sect2.para: DER stands for Distinguished Encoding Rules. This format is also quite often used on MS Windows system as well as with Java. This is a binary format so it cannot directly be viewed as a text file (in opposite from the pem format).
Convert an existing certificate in PEM format to the equivalent DER format is straight forward using openssl
sect2.screen: $> openssl x509 -inform pem -in certificate.pem -outform der \ -out certificate.der

sect2.title: PKCS #12 format
sect2.para: PKCS stands for Public-Key Cryptography Standards and #12 is a format in which both a private and a public key is stored in the same file for the purpose of authentication.

The PKCS format is part of a larger set of standards defined by the RSA Laboratories. Some of these standard are also defined as RFCs. This specific standard (#12) is a format used to store client certificates. Client certificates are used in analogy to server certificates but to identify the client and not a server. A server can for example be setup in such a way that a client must have a trusted certificate in order to connect to the server. The server trusts a specific certificate if the certificate have been signed by an authority accepted by the server.
It would bring to far to go through all the details of this format here. However this type of format is handled by the pkcs12 subcommand to openssl command.
To create a client certificate to be used for authentication based on a existing key-pair use the command
One difference here is that the client certificate will be protected by a password so this will have to be given when the certificate is created (openssl will ask for it).
In order to view some details an existing client certificate use the following command
sect2.screen: $> openssl pkcs12 -noout -info -in myclcert.p12 Enter Import Password: <SECRET_PASSWORD> MAC Iteration 2048 MAC verified OK PKCS7 Encrypted data: pbeWithSHA1And40BitRC2-CBC, Iteration 2048 Certificate bag PKCS7 Data Shrouded Keybag: pbeWithSHA1And3-KeyTripleDES-CBC, Iteration 2048
sect2.para: In the output there is a statements about "MAC verified OK". In this context MAC stands for Message Authentication Code and is a way to guarantee that the certificate is valid and has not been tampered with. The reference to PKCS #7 refers to specific message syntax which is detailed in RFC2315

sect1.title: Certification Revocation List (CRL) and OCSP
sect1.para: One thing that we haven't yet touched upon is the directory crl/ under the apache configuration directory. This directory is used to store a Certificate Revocation List. Basically a list of certificates that the issuer might revoked and should no longer be trusted. From the server perspective this is used to verify that any certificate a client might present is still valid.

The problem with such a revocation list is that it must be constantly renewed to be of any value. In addition both the client and the server needs to have access to an updated revocation lists since neither part can really trust the other part.

For the reason with the need of constant updates of the revocation lists this has too large extent been replaced by online direct checking using what is known as OCSP (Online Certificate Status Protocol). Basically the client will verify any certificate given by the server by going online and check a central revocation lists on a dedicated certificate server.

Ideally all official root certificates (CA certificates) will have ps59D7005DKsuch a server. So for example if a server claims to have a certificate verified by, say, Verisign the client will go online to the Verisign OCSP server and double check that the certificate is really still valid.

We will not discuss this any further in this tutorial but should the need to setup a certificate server arise the open source server "OpenCA" (http://www.openca.org/\) server might be good candidate to examine since it also includes a OCSPD server daemon.

sect1.title: Summary
sect1.para: With the above steps we have created the key-pairs we need for both the Web-server as well as the mail servers (Dovecot2 and postfix). You should now take a backup of this directory and keep it in a safe place. When you later on upgrade your servers you should restore these certificates to avoid client warnings.

Since there is quite a lot of text in the previous section we just repeat the actual commands below that we used to create the key-pairs to make it clearer that it is not that difficult. Each command set first creates the key-pair and then signs it.

caution.para: Remember to uncomment and set the “subjectAltName” in the configuration file if you want your certificates to be valid for multi-homed servers, i.e. servers that are accessed with several different DNS names (but only one IP-address).

sect2.title: Creating the CA (root certificate)
sect2.screen: $> openssl req -new -keyout private/ca_private.pem \ -out csr/ca_public_req.pem -config ./our_openssl.cnf $> openssl ca -create_serial -out public/ca_public.pem \ -selfsign -extensions v3_ca -config our_openssl.cnf \ -days 7000 -infiles csr/ca_public_req.pem

sect2.title: Creating the Apache HTTPS certificate
sect2.screen: $> openssl req -new -nodes -keyout private/https_private.pem \ -out csr/https_public_req.pem -config ./our_openssl.cnf $> openssl ca -out public/https_public.pem -config ./our_openssl.cnf \ -infiles csr/https_public_req.pem

sect2.title: Creating the mail certificate
sect2.screen: $> openssl req -new -nodes -keyout private/mail_private.pem \ -out csr/mail_public_req.pem -config ./our_openssl.cnf $> openssl ca -out public/mail_public.pem -config ./our_openssl.cnf \ -infiles csr/mail_public_req.pem
